questions.question_text: Among the following options, which statements is Accurate regarding neuropsychiatric symptoms in Huntington’s disease?

options.text: Psychosis is the most common neuropsychiatric symptom.
Irritability and depression may present several years prior to onset of motor symptoms. 184 • PSYCHIATRY
The suicide rate among individuals with Huntington’s disease is 25%.
Symptoms worsen with duration of the disease.
The predominant cognitive symptom is attentional dysfunction.

correct_answer.text: Irritability and depression may present several years prior to onset of motor symptoms. 184 • PSYCHIATRY

questions.explanation: Irritability and depression may present several years before the onset of motor symptoms. The suicide rate among patients with Huntington’s disease is around 7%, and suicidal ideation among mutation carriers is around 20%. The most common symptoms are depression, apathy, irritability, and anxiety. Symptoms do not correlate with duration of the disease and can be seen very early in the course of illness. Re FeRe NCeS Di Maio, L., Squitieri, F., Napolitano, G., et al. (1993). Onset symptoms in 510 patients with Huntington’s disease. Journal of Medical Genetics, 30,

questions.question_text: In HIV-associated neurocognitive disorder in a patient on long-term ART, which finding is typically seen?

options.text: Continued elevation of CD8 count that does not normalize
Complete normalization of CD4 count in all patients
Elimination of viral replication in the brain

correct_answer.text: Continued elevation of CD8 count that does not normalize

questions.explanation: CD8+ T-cell counts remain elevated during HIV infection and do not normalize despite long-term combined antiretroviral therapy, while CD4+ counts may normalize with early treatment initiation.

questions.question_text: In familial FTD, the pathological findings typically show:
questions.explanation: Familial FTD is characterised by Tau-negative, Ubiquitin-positive pathology, which distinguishes it from Pick's disease (Tau-positive, Ubiquitin-positive).

The physician notes to herself that the patient has substantial cognitive impairment and features suggestive of the diagnosis of major neurocognitive disorder due to Huntington’s disease, but she is not sure about the cause of the neurocognitive disorder. She also notes that the patient’s son appears extremely anxious. She has a tight schedule and cannot provide a counseling session for the patient’s son until the next day. What is the most suitable diagnosis to record on the insurance claim form that the patient’s son will submit on his father’s behalf?

questions.explanation: The category unspecified neurocognitive disorder applies to presentations in which symptoms characteristic of a neurocognitive disorder that cause clinically significant distress or impairment in social, occupational, or other important areas of functioning predominate but do not meet the full criteria for any of the disorders in the neurocognitive disorders diagnostic class. The unspecified neurocognitive disorder category is also used in situations in which the precise etiology cannot be determined with sufficient certainty to make an etiological attribution. In this case, Huntington’s disease is suspected but not established. “Unspecified CNS disorder” is not a DSM-5 diagnosis and would be inadequately specific to the patient’s condition. The apparent severity of the deficits precludes a diagnosis of mild neurocognitive disorder or a V code designation of problem related to living alone.

questions.question_text: A previously healthy 67-year-old man, who is experiencing an acute change in mental status, is brought to the emergency department by his family. There is no evidence in the initial history, physical examination, and laboratory studies to indicate substance intoxication or withdrawal, or to suggest another medical problem as the cause of his altered mental state. Over the course of 1 hour of observation, his level of alertness varies from alert but distractible, with apparent auditory and visual hallucinations, to somnolent; he has difficulty sustaining attention to an examiner, and he cannot perform simple tasks such as serial subtractions or spelling words backwards. What is the most suitable diagnosis?

options.text: A diagnosis of major neurocognitive disorder due to Alzheimer's disease.
Delirium due to another medical condition.

questions.explanation: This man meets criteria for some sort of delirium, but at this point in the course of his illness it cannot be determined what the cause is. The “unspecified delirium” category can be used when the clinician chooses not to specify a specific cause, when the diagnostic criteria for delirium are not entirely fulfilled, or when the specific diagnostic subtype of delirium cannot be ascertained.

questions.question_text: At what age is early-onset Alzheimer's disease typically diagnosed?
questions.explanation: Early-onset Alzheimer's disease is typically diagnosed before the age of 60-65 years, with some definitions using before 65 as the cutoff.

questions.question_text: Major and mild neurocognitive disorders (NCDs) exist on a spectrum of cognitive and functional impairment. which of the following options constitutes an important threshold differentiating the two diagnoses?

options.text: Whether the patient is a poor historian regarding cognitive changes.
Whether there is objective evidence of cognitive decline compared to the patient's previous level of functioning.
Whether or not the cognitive impairment is sufficient to interfere with independent completion of activities of daily living.
Whether or not the cognitive deficits occur exclusively in the context of a delirium.
Whether or not the cognitive deficits are better explained by another mental disorder.

correct_answer.text: Whether or not the cognitive impairment is sufficient to interfere with independent completion of activities of daily living.

questions.explanation: Criterion B for major or mild NCD relates to the individual’s level of independence in everyday functioning. Individuals with major NCD will have impairment of sufficient severity to interfere with independence, such that others will have to take over tasks that the individuals were previously able to complete on their own. Individuals with mild NCD will have preserved independence, although there may be subtle interference with function or a report that tasks require more effort or take more time than previously. The distinction between major and mild NCD is inherently arbitrary, and the disorders exist along a continuum. Precise thresholds are therefore difficult to determine. Careful history taking, observation, and integration with other findings are required, and the implications of diagnosis should be considered when an individual’s clinical manifestations lie at a boundary. For both mild and major NCD, Criterion A requires evidence of a cognitive decline based on 1) concern on the part of the patient, a knowledgeable informant, or a clinician that there has been such a decline; and 2) impairment in cognitive performance as documented by standardized testing or other objective assessment. For major NCD, significant decline and substantial impairment are specified; for mild NCD, the words modest and mild are used. Both disorders can occur with comorbid delirium, but they cannot be diagnosed if the cognitive impairment occurs only in the context of delirium (Criterion C). Both disorders can occur in patients with other significant disorders, but in order to make the diagnosis, the cognitive deficits must not be primarily attributable to another disorder (Criterion D).

questions.question_text: Among the following, which is most commonly seen intracranial opportunistic infection in HIV?
questions.explanation: Toxoplasmosis is the most common opportunistic infection seen in AIDS patients. They may present with focal or diffuse cognitive or affective symptoms. Imaging may help with the diagnosis but may be normal in many cases. Defi nitive diagnosis is by biopsy. Cryptococcosis presents as meningitis with headache and fever. Other viral infections of the brain may present with personality and behavioural changes. HSV encephalitis typically presents with temporal lobe symptoms. CMV infection presents as encephalitis, retinitis, and peripheral neuropathies with demyelination. Progressive multifocal leucoencephalopathy is caused by a papova virus. The prognosis is poor. Hales RE and Yudofsky SC. The American Psychiatric Publishing Textbook of Neuropsychiatry and Clinical Neurosciences, 4th edn. American Psychiatric Press, 2002, p. 787.

questions.question_text: In HIV-associated neurocognitive disorder in a patient on long-term ART, what finding is typically seen?

options.text: High CD4 count with normalized CD8 count
High CD8 count that does not normalize despite ART

correct_answer.text: High CD8 count that does not normalize despite ART

questions.explanation: Despite long-term antiretroviral therapy (ART), CD8+ T-cell counts remain elevated and do not normalize. While CD4+ counts may return to near-normal levels (>500 cells/mm³) with ART, CD8+ counts persistently remain elevated. Additionally, cortical, subcortical, gray matter, and white matter atrophy may continue despite ART, and neuronal loss can persist.

questions.question_text: LRRK2 mutation is seen in which condition?
questions.explanation: LRRK2 mutation is seen in Parkinson disease and is located on chromosome 12p11.2. Other genetic mutations associated with Parkinson disease include PINK, PARKIN, and SNCA.

questions.question_text: Among the following options, which HLA haplotypes is MOST often noted to be positive in individuals with narcolepsy?
questions.explanation: HLADQ and HLADR are two alleles that are found in about 85% of patients with narcolepsy. These alleles are found in 15% to 35% of the general population.

questions.question_text: Wernicke's aphasia is what type?
questions.explanation: Wernicke's aphasia is fluent or receptive aphasia, located in Broadmann's area 22 in the superior temporal lobe, characterized by fluent but meaningless speech with comprehension deficits.

questions.question_text: Which is the most important clinical feature that defines delirium?
questions.explanation: The core defining feature of delirium is a disturbance in attention and awareness, often with acute onset and fluctuation. While agitation and disorientation may occur, they are not the defining feature.

questions.question_text: Frontotemporal dementia is associated with intracellular accumulation of which proteins?
questions.explanation: Frontotemporal dementia is associated with intracellular accumulations of tau and ubiquitin.

questions.question_text: What type of aphasia is Wernicke's aphasia characterized as?
questions.explanation: Wernicke's aphasia is characterized as fluent aphasia, with patients producing speech that is grammatically fluent but lacks meaningful content.

questions.question_text: Among the following, which condition is linked to intractable epilepsy, autism-like features and skin lesions in children?

options.text: A diagnosis of fragile X syndrome
A diagnosis of foetal alcohol syndrome

questions.explanation: Tuberous sclerosis is an autosomal dominant genetic multisystem disorder characterised by widespread hamartomas in the brain, heart, skin, eyes, kidney, lung, and liver. Most features of tuberous sclerosis become evident only in childhood after 3 years of age. The affected genes TSC1 and TSC encode for proteins hamartin and tuberin respectively. Epilepsy is seen in 60–80% tuberous sclerosis cases and is thought to be secondary to changes of GABA receptors in dysplastic neurons, and enhanced excitation via glutamate receptors in cortical hamartomas. The epilepsy is generally of an early onset and is often intractable in severity. Hypomelanotic macules are the most common dermatological manifestation; they are seen in 90–98% of patients with tuberous sclerosis. Curatolo P, Bombardieri R and Jozwiak S. Tuberous sclerosis. Lancet; 372: 657–668.

questions.question_text: Which pathological finding is characteristic of familial frontotemporal dementia?
questions.explanation:
In familial frontotemporal dementia, the three most common genetic causes are C9orf72, GRN (progranulin), and MAPT. C9orf72 (the most common hereditary cause in Caucasians) and GRN mutations both produce TDP-43-positive, tau-negative neuropathology, which is ubiquitin-positive on immunostaining. 
GRN mutations are over three times more frequent than MAPT mutations in hereditary FTD. Therefore the characteristic pathological finding in familial FTD overall is tau-negative, ubiquitin-positive inclusions .

questions.question_text: Stereotypical non-goal-directed movements seen in Parkinson's disease are best described as:
questions.explanation: Punding is characterized as stereotypical motor behaviour with intense fascination involving repetitive, excessive, and non-goal-oriented handling and examining of objects, commonly seen in Parkinson's disease with dopamine replacement therapy.

questions.question_text: In which of the following dementias is REM sleep behaviour disorder a core feature?
questions.explanation: REM sleep behaviour disorder, characterised by dream-enacting behaviours with vocal sounds and sudden violent movements during REM sleep, is a core feature of Dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB) and can precede cognitive decline by several years.

questions.question_text: Among the following, which has been found to be effective in the treatment of pathological laughing and crying (PLAC) syndrome?
questions.explanation: Pathological emotions are characterized by episodes of laughing or crying, or both, that are not appropriate to the context. They may be spontaneous or triggered by non-emotional events. Pathological emotions have classically been explained as secondary to the bilateral interruption of descending neocortical upper motor neuron innervations of bulbar motor nuclei. Some patients with pathological emotions have bilateral lesions and pseudobulbar palsy, but others do not. Most recently, the frontopontocerebellar pathways have been implicated in the pathogenesis of pathological emotions. It is seen in about 15% of patients with stroke. Citalopram, as well as nortriptyline, have been found to be effective in the treatment of pathological crying after stroke in randomized placebo-controlled trials. In addition, post-stroke depression and PLAC appear to be independent phenomena, although they may coexist. Kaplan HI. Kaplan and Sadock’s Comprehensive Textbook of Psychiatry, 8th edn. Lippincott Williams and Wilkins, 2004, p. 361.

questions.question_text: Which infectious disease, when treated, is commonly associated with iatrogenic depression as a complication?
questions.explanation: Hepatitis C is commonly associated with depression when treated with interferons, which are known to cause depressive symptoms as a side effect. This is a well-documented complication of interferon-alpha therapy for chronic hepatitis C.

questions.question_text: A 35-year-old man presents to his physician complaining of persistent anxiety, poor sleep, and feelings of hopelessness for the past two months. He reports that these symptoms began shortly after his wife abruptly filed for divorce. While he manages to complete his basic tasks at work, he admits he is highly distracted, makes frequent errors, and has completely withdrawn from his friends. He denies any thoughts of self-harm, changes in appetite, or anhedonia. He has no history of head trauma or physical assault, and he does not experience nightmares or flashbacks. A complete neurological examination is unremarkable, showing normal muscle tone and no involuntary movements.
questions.explanation: Adjustment disorder is characterized by the development of emotional or behavioral symptoms in response to an identifiable psychosocial stressor (in this case, the sudden divorce) occurring within 3 months of the stressor\'s onset. The patient\'s symptoms cause marked distress and impairment in social and occupational functioning (withdrawing from friends, making errors at work), but do not meet the full criteria for another mental disorder (like Major Depressive Disorder, as he lacks anhedonia, appetite changes, and suicidal ideation).

questions.question_text: Enzyme deficient in acute intermittent porphyria:
questions.explanation: Acute intermittent porphyria is characterized by partial deficiency of hydroxymethylbilane synthase (HMBS), also known as porphobilinogen deaminase, which leads to accumulation of porphyrin precursors and neuropsychiatric manifestations.

questions.question_text: What is simultagnosia?

options.text: Inability to recognize simultaneous visual stimuli, seeing only one object at a time

correct_answer.text: Inability to recognize simultaneous visual stimuli, seeing only one object at a time

questions.explanation: Simultagnosia is the inability to recognize simultaneous visual stimuli in a visual scene, with patients able to perceive only one object at a time despite intact basic visual function.

questions.question_text: Mr Williams is a 70 year old man who has presented to his GP with difficulty co-ordinating the movements of his right arm. Which of the following neurodegenerative disorders is most likely to be responsible?
questions.explanation: Corticobasal degeneration is a rare, progressive neurodegenerative disease involving the cerebral cortex and the basal ganglia. The movement symptoms typically appear asymmetrically and include apraxia, aphasia, parkinsonism and alien hand syndrome.

questions.question_text: What would be the most probable explanation for the individual’s presentation?

options.text: A diagnosis of advancing Parkinson’s disease
A diagnosis of major neurocognitive disorder

questions.explanation: Delirium presents with an acute change in mental status accompanied by inattention, reduced awareness of surroundings, at least one additional cognitive deficit, and often a range of behavioral, emotional, and personality symptoms. It is frequently misdiagnosed as depression, other psychiatric disorders, or dementia. About 40% of psychiatry consults in the general hospital for depression

questions.question_text: Which cells are least likely to be directly invaded by HIV in the brain?
questions.explanation: HIV does not directly invade neurons but infects glial cells (microglia, macrophages) and perivascular macrophages that support and protect neurons, indirectly affecting neuronal function through inflammation.

questions.question_text: Among the options below, which one consistently differentiates Lambert– Eaton myasthenic syndrome (LEMS) from myasthenia gravis?

options.text: Ocular myasthenia gravis does not respond to anticholinesterase inhibitors.
Repeated stimulation of motor neurons in myasthenia gravis yields decreasing motor responses.
Younger individuals typically present with LEMS.
Muscle power increases with sustained contraction in myasthenia gravis.
Unlike myasthenia gravis, LEMS is often linked to a tumor.

correct_answer.text: Repeated stimulation of motor neurons in myasthenia gravis yields decreasing motor responses.

questions.explanation: Myasthenia gravis presents with ptosis in 25% of cases. In 80% of cases, there is antibody against skeletal muscle nicotinic acetylcholine receptor. The disease has gradual onset with progressive course and can present at any age. It is associated with thymic tumor, thyrotoxicosis, rheumatoid arthritis, and systemic lupus erythematosus. Sustained contraction of the affected muscle leads to temporary weakness. LEMS, on the other hand, is a paraneoplastic syndrome and has an association with autoimmune conditions such as pernicious anemia. Proximal muscles are involved; extraocular muscles are spared. Muscle power steadily increases with sustained contraction. The cause is attributed to an antibody that crossreacts with tumor antigens and voltagegated calcium channels involved in acetylcholine release. This, in turn, leads to presynaptic neuromuscular transmission. On electromyogram, muscle responses decrease in response to repeated stimulation in myasthenia gravis but increase in LEMS.

questions.question_text: Defective copper metabolism due to a defect in chromosome 13 characterizes which condition?
questions.explanation: Wilson disease is an autosomal recessive condition of defective copper metabolism due to a defect in chromosome 13, characterized by hepatic symptoms followed by psychiatric symptoms and choreoathetosis affecting the lenticular nuclei.

questions.question_text: Mrs Pamela West is a 75-year-old woman who has presented to her GP with tremor and difficulty walking. Her husband has noted that her face often does not respond when she is told about happy or sad news. Which of the following is associated with this condition?
questions.explanation: Parkinson's disease is characterised by the cell death of dopaminergic neurones in the basal ganglia, Lewy bodies (alpha synuclein). The LRRK2 mutation is associated with some cases of Parkinson's disease.

questions.question_text: A migraineur comes to the emergency room with severe headache, photophobia, and blurry vision in both eyes. Intraocular pressure was elevated at 72/ 67 mm Hg in both eyes. Which medication is the likely cause of this presentation?
questions.explanation: Topiramate is indicated for epilepsy and migraine treatment (prophylaxis). However, it has many offlabel indications, including treatment of alcohol use disorder, binge eating disorder, posttraumatic stress disorder, essential tremor, and weight loss. Topiramate is the only anticonvulsant that can cause angleclosure glaucoma. Typical onset of glaucoma occurs within a month of topiramate initiation. 168 • PSYChIAtRY Patients should be educated to discontinue topiramate in the case of decreased visual acuity and ocular pain. Other medications that can cause this presentation include anticholinergics, antihistamines, diuretics, and tricyclic antidepressants. Sumatriptan can cause visual disturbances but not acute angleclosure glaucoma.

questions.question_text: Which is a human prion disease?
questions.explanation: Fatal familial insomnia is a human prion disease, along with sporadic Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (sCJD), variant CJD (vCJD), Kuru, and Gerstmann-Sträussler-Scheinker syndrome.

questions.question_text: Preventive treatment for cluster headache includes verapamil or which of the following?

options.text: 100% oxygen at 10 to 12 L via face mask

questions.explanation: Verapamil and lithium are commonly used as preventive agents for cluster headache. In fact, unlike in migraine, cluster headaches are commonly headache free with prophylaxis.

questions.question_text: A 25yearold male patient exhibits bilateral thigh weakness for 1 week and inability to walk for a day. He had an episode of gastroenteritis 1 month ago. He reports racing heart and sweating. On examination, knee and ankle reflexes are diminished on both of the lower extremities. Both thighs are weak, and he has hypoesthesia over his legs. CSF examination shows tION OF N EUROLOGICAL DISORDERS • 149 increased albumin and normal cell count. Which of the following correlates with musclewasting and hence poor clinical outlook?
questions.explanation: The above clinical picture is of acute idiopathic polyneuropathy or Guillain– Barré syndrome (GBS), which occurs in two forms: demyelinating variant (common in the United States) and axonal variant (common in China). The disease usually presents with symmetric ascending paralysis, more pronounced in proximal lower extremity muscles. Deep tendon reflexes are typically absent. Affected individuals may also experience symptoms of autonomic dysfunction such as sweating or palpitations (cardiac arrhythmia). The disease is often preceded by recent infection or surgery. CSF classically shows elevated albumin level and a normal or nearnormal cell count (socalled cytoalbuminologic dissociation). Electromyography reveals motor and sensory conduction slowing suggestive of demyelination or axonal loss. Musclewasting typically develops when axonal degeneration has occurred. Overall, 70% of the cases resolve completely, 25% of affected patients are left with residual paralysis, and 5% die, largely due to respiratory muscle involvement. Symptoms usually decrease and disappear by the 4th weak into the illness. Advanced age, Campylobacter jejuni infection, acute onset of symptoms, and axonal degeneration are poor prognostic factors.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements about confabulation is correct?

options.text: Can only occur in Korsakoff syndrome
There is deliberate falsification of facts
It is associated with ventromedial frontal lobe pathology
There is subjective awareness of memory impairment

correct_answer.text: It is associated with ventromedial frontal lobe pathology

questions.explanation: Confabulation is associated with ventromedial frontal lobe pathology; the New Oxford Textbook of Psychiatry (p.423) states: \'The link with frontal lobe pathology, particularly in the ventro-medial region, has been established in many investigations,\' and this is further corroborated by Organic Psychiatry (pp.42–43). Option A is wrong because confabulation is not restricted to Korsakoff syndrome — this is a common misconception explicitly refuted in the passages. Option B is wrong because confabulation, as defined by Berlyne (1972), occurs \'in clear consciousness,\' not exclusively in clouded states. Option C is wrong because confabulation is an organically derived falsification of memory without deliberate intent. Option E is wrong because patients who confabulate characteristically lack subjective awareness of their memory errors.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is NOT a characteristic of confabulation?

options.text: There is subjective awareness of memory impairment

questions.explanation: Confabulation is a falsification of memory occurring in clear consciousness associated with organic states. It does not occur in clouded consciousness; it specifically occurs when consciousness is clear. Autobiographical memory is often affected, and there may be subjective awareness of confabulation.

questions.question_text: A 45yearold male patient exhibits headaches, irritability, and aggressiveness for a few months along with recentonset weakness of the left lower extremity. On examination, he has loss of vibration sense in the left lower extremity and loss of pain and temperature in the right lower extremity. He walks with an ataxic gait. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the thoracic spinal cord is normal, but brain MRI reveals punctate areas of infarction in deep white matter in the frontal lobe. Which of the following would be an appropriate next step in investigating the cause?

options.text: MRI with gadolinium contrast of brain

questions.explanation: The patient presents with features suspicious for syphilitic arteritis resulting from meningovascular syphilis (MVS). MVS occurs usually within 5 years of initial infection. It presents with subacute headache, behavioral changes (frontal lobe involvement), and spinal cord involvement. The progressive form may present with strokelike symptoms, with clinical features reflecting the specific affected bloodsupply region. Acute spinal cord infarcts may present with myelopathy, hemiplegic symptoms (Brown– Sequard syndrome), or transverse myelitis. Mediumsized penetrating arteries are most commonly involved, causing tION OF N EUROLOGICAL DISORDERS • 145 punctate deep white matter lesions on MRI of the brain. MRI of the spinal cord could be normal or show T2 hyperintensities.

questions.question_text: A 28yearold prison inmate was brought to the emergency room after he had been confused and disoriented for a day and a half. He complained of seeing small animals on the floor, which were not real. On evaluation he was disoriented to person and place. His pupils are equal, round, and reactive to light and accommodation. His blood alcohol level and urine toxicology screen are negative. Routine blood tests are within normal limits. During mental status evaluation, he was asked, “What is the capital of the United States?” and responded, “New York.” No focal neurological signs are found, and electroencephalogram reveals normal awake tracings. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation: According to the US Department of Education, in 2012– 2013 children received special education most commonly for a specific learning disability such as in math, reading, or writing. Specific learning disability was the cause for 35% of patients in special education. Autism accounted for 8%, intellectual disability accounted for 7%, emotional disturbance accounted for 6%, and ADHD under the classification of “other health impairment” accounted for 12% of patients in special education.

questions.question_text: Mrs June Murphy is a 69-year-old woman who has presented to her GP with difficulty swallowing and a change in her voice. She is diagnosed with bulbar palsy following an MRI. Which of the following is she most likely to have?
questions.explanation: Bulbar palsy refers to a range of different signs and symptoms linked to impairment of function of the cranial nerves 9, 10, 11 and 12 which occurs due to a lower motor neuron lesion in the medulla oblongata or from lesions of the lower cranial nerves outside the brainstem. The eyes are not typically affected and the jaw jerk is absent or reduced. The tongue is commonly atrophic and shows fasciculations.

questions.question_text: Familial FTD with autosomal dominant inheritance shows which pattern?
questions.explanation: Familial frontotemporal dementia shows tau negativity with ubiquitin positivity in the pathological inclusions.

questions.question_text: All of the below options apply features of hyperactive delirium help differentiate it from hypoactive delirium, with the exception of
questions.explanation: Hyperactive delirium is characterized by increased activity levels, including restlessness, loss of control of activities, and increased speed of action. Hypoactive delirium on the other hand is characterized by decreased activity levels including apathy, listlessness, and decreased speed of action. Hyperactive delirium may present with pressure of speech, altered content, and aggression, whereas hypoactive delirium usually presents with a decreased amount of speech and hypersomnolence. Hyperactive delirium is said to have a better prognosis than hypoactive delirium. But both types of delirium are characterized by diffuse slowing on the EEG. Hales RE and Yudofsky SC. The American Psychiatric Publishing Textbook of Neuropsychiatry and Clinical Neurosciences, 4th edn. American Psychiatric Press 2002, p. 543.

questions.question_text: Among the following options, which is least likely to present with apathy, executive dysfunction, and forgetfulness?

options.text: A diagnosis of frontotemporal neurocognitive disorder
Neurocognitive disorder due to HIV infection

questions.explanation: Apathy, executive dysfunction, and forgetfulness are suggestive of frontal lobe pathology and would be unlikely in a patient with a parietal lesion.

questions.question_text: Which organism is implicated in Prion disease?
questions.explanation: Fatal Familial Insomnia is a human prion disease, along with others like sCJD, vCJD, Kuru, and Gerstmann-Sträussler-Scheinker syndrome.

questions.question_text: A 62yearold male patient comes to a neurologist for frequent falls. Exam is notable for vertical gaze palsy and bradykinesia. The neurologist orders magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), which is notable for dorsal midbrain atrophy. This presentation is most consistent with which diagnosis?

options.text: A diagnosis of shy– Drager syndrome

questions.explanation: Progressive supranuclear palsy classically presents with vertical gaze palsy, symmetrical rigidity, bradykinesia, and frequent falls. MRI may demonstrate atrophy of the dorsal midbrain. Patients may also demonstrate dysarthria, dysphagia, and frontal cognitive deficits.

questions.question_text: Among the following options, which vitamin deficiencies can present as a hematologic disorder with neuropsychiatric manifestations, including apathy, irritability, cognitive impairment, psychosis, and delirium?
questions.explanation: Cobalamin (vitamin B12) deficiency is characterized by the development of a chronic macrocytic anemia with neurological and psychiatric manifestations that include peripheral neuropathy, apathy, irritability, and depression. Delirium, with associated dementia or psychosis, may also be seen.

questions.question_text: A 34-year-old woman being treated for seizures has irregular menstrual periods, at which time her seizures worsen. It is most likely that she has which of the following?
questions.explanation: Catamenial epilepsy describes a worsening of seizures in relation to the menstrual cycle, affecting approximately 40% of women with epilepsy. Hormonal fluctuations in estrogen and progesterone during specific menstrual phases trigger increased seizure frequency.

questions.question_text: Which of the following gait patterns is characteristic of Huntington's disease?
questions.explanation: Huntington's disease is associated with a chaotic gait pattern, which distinguishes it from other movement disorders such as parkinsonian shuffling or cerebellar broad-based ataxic gaits.

questions.question_text: What is ideomotor apraxia?

options.text: Inability to perform learned purposeful movements despite intact motor function

correct_answer.text: Inability to perform learned purposeful movements despite intact motor function

questions.explanation: Ideomotor apraxia is the inability to perform learned purposeful movements on command despite intact motor and sensory function, often demonstrated by asking patients to mime actions like hammering.

questions.question_text: A 37yearold male patient comes to his neurologist with a 1year history of motor symptoms, including involuntary jerky movements of the pelvis, limbs, and trunk with unsteady gait. For several months he has also experienced worsening cognitive function and depression. His father had similar symptoms in his early 40s. The most likely genetic basis of this disease is:

options.text: Huntingtin gene with excessive CAG repeats

correct_answer.text: Huntingtin gene with excessive CAG repeats

questions.explanation: This patient most likely has major neurocognitive disorder due to Huntington disease. This gene, which encodes the protein huntingtin (with an i), is found on the short arm of chromosome

questions.question_text: Which CSF biomarker is decreased in Alzheimer's disease?
questions.explanation: Amyloid-beta 42 is decreased in Alzheimer's disease CSF due to deposition in amyloid plaques in the brain.

questions.question_text: Prevalence of psychosis in DiGeorge syndrome.
questions.explanation: Schizophrenia is most strongly associated with DiGeorge syndrome, with up to 30% of those with DiGeorge syndrome developing a psychotic illness, representing a significantly elevated risk compared to the general population.

questions.question_text: Among the following options, which is the first to improve with treatment in individuals with normal pressure hydrocephalus?
questions.explanation: Normal pressure hydrocephalus (NPH) is characterized by dementia, urinary incontinence (urgency and frequency), and gait apraxia. Vision is not typically impaired in NPH. Gait apraxia is the initial, most consistent, and most prominent feature of NPH. Gait apraxia is also the first to improve with treatment.

questions.question_text: Which pathological finding is characteristic of Alzheimer's disease?
questions.explanation: The primary pathological hallmarks of Alzheimer's disease are beta amyloid plaques and neurofibrillary tangles containing ubiquitin. While alpha synuclein is associated with Parkinson's disease and Lewy body dementia, beta amyloid and ubiquitin are the characteristic pathological findings in Alzheimer's disease.

questions.question_text: Wernicke's aphasia is characterized by which of the following?

options.text: Fluent speech with impaired comprehension and repetition
Fluent agrammatical speech with intact comprehension
Global aphasia affecting all language functions

correct_answer.text: Fluent speech with impaired comprehension and repetition

questions.explanation: Wernicke's aphasia is a fluent aphasia with impaired comprehension and repetition, often described as wordy speech contrasting with Broca's broken speech.

questions.question_text: Which neurodegenerative disorder is linked to schizophrenia?
questions.explanation: Schizophrenia and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) show positive genetic and transcriptomic correlation with overlapped gene expression profiles.

questions.question_text: Prion diseases are characterized by which histopathological feature?
questions.explanation: Prion diseases are characterized by protein misfolding, where normal prion proteins (PrP) misfold into pathogenic forms that accumulate in the brain, causing neurodegenerative disease.

questions.question_text: Confabulation in Korsakoff's syndrome occurs under which circumstances?

options.text: Impaired autobiographical memory with subjective awareness of deficit
Impaired autobiographical memory without intentional falsification and without awareness of memory loss

correct_answer.text: Impaired autobiographical memory without intentional falsification and without awareness of memory loss

questions.explanation: In Korsakoff's syndrome, confabulation is not intentional falsification but rather the filling of memory gaps. There is impaired autobiographical memory and characteristically no subjective awareness of the memory deficit.

questions.question_text: A 9yearold child develops worsening headache, especially in the morning, accompanied by vomiting without nausea. MRI with gadolinium reveals enhancing tumor within the fourth ventricle. Microscopic examination reveals the presence of dense, round blue cells. What is the best treatment for this condition?

options.text: Combination of surgery, radiation treatment, and chemotherapy

correct_answer.text: Combination of surgery, radiation treatment, and chemotherapy

questions.explanation: Medulloblastoma accounts for 30% of pediatric brain tumors and is the most common malignant brain tumor in children. Initial symptoms are caused by increased intracranial pressure, and children usually experience headache upon awakening and progressive vomiting without nausea. Hypercellularity and round blue cells on histologic examination are diagnostic. A combination of surgery, radiation, and chemotherapy offers the best outcome. The 5year survival rate for children with averagerisk disease is 70% to 80%.

questions.question_text: Taupathy is associated with which conditions?
questions.explanation: Taupathy refers to pathological accumulation of tau protein and includes FTD with Pick bodies, Alzheimer's disease, progressive supranuclear palsy, corticobasal degeneration, and dementia pugilistica.

questions.question_text: An 85yearold female patient presented to her neurologist for 6 months of worsening memory. For the past 8 years the neurologist has been treating the female patient for motor symptoms, including tremor, rigidity, and slow movements. The neurologist notes that her Mini Mental State Examination score is 6 points lower than it was at her baseline evaluation 5 years ago. More intensive neuropsychological evaluation reveals deficits in the areas of visuospatial and executive function. The most likely diagnosis of her cognitive impairment is:

options.text: Major neurocognitive disorder due to progressive supranuclear palsy
Mild neurocognitive disorder due to Alzheimer disease
Major neurocognitive disorder due to corticobasal degeneration
Major neurocognitive disorder due to Parkinson disease
A diagnosis of major frontotemporal neurocognitive disorder

correct_answer.text: Major neurocognitive disorder due to Parkinson disease

questions.explanation: This patient most likely has Parkinson disease based on the triad of tremor, rigidity, and bradykinesia. Major neurocognitive disorder due to Parkinson disease is a common, gradually developing complication of the condition, particularly as the patient ages and the disease progresses. Although this form of dementia is on the synucleinopathy spectrum of major neurocognitive disorder with Lewy bodies, a key distinguishing feature is that motor symptoms appear first in major neurocognitive disorder due to Parkinson disease.

questions.question_text: Which malignancy is classically associated with NMDA receptor encephalitis?
questions.explanation: NMDA receptor encephalitis is strongly associated with ovarian teratoma, particularly in younger female patients, though other malignancies and seronegative cases also occur.

questions.question_text: Among the following options, which psychiatric symptoms is a core diagnostic feature of major neurocognitive disorder with Lewy bodies?
questions.explanation: The core diagnostic features of major neurocognitive disorder with Lewy bodies are (A) fluctuating cognition with pronounced variations in attention and alertness, (B) recurrent visual hallucinations that are well formed and detailed, and (C) spontaneous features of parkinsonism with onset subsequent to the development of cognitive decline. questions.question_text: What are the characteristic pathological findings in chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE)?
questions.explanation: Chronic traumatic encephalopathy is characterized by accumulation of hyperphosphorylated tau, particularly in perivascular regions and at the depths of cortical sulci.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is NOT a component of Gerstmann syndrome?
questions.explanation: Damage to the inferior parietal lobule of the dominant hemisphere results in Gerstmann's syndrome. It is characterized by four primary symptoms: a) Dysgraphia/agraphia: deficiency in the ability to write b) Dyscalculia/acalculia: difficulty in learning or comprehending mathematics c) Finger agnosia: inability to distinguish the fingers on the hand d) Left-right disorientation

questions.question_text: Which medication has the strongest evidence in support of its ability to reduce the relapse rate of relapsing– remitting multiple sclerosis?
questions.explanation: Natalizumab is an alpha4 integrin antibody, used in treatment of relapsing– remitting multiple sclerosis. Rarely it can cause progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy. Its use is limited to relapsingremitting patients who responded poorly to interferon and/ or glatiramer tION OF N EUROLOGICAL DISORDERS • 147 acetate or relapsingremitting patients with severe initial course. Intravenous immunoglobulin might reduce relapse rate, but there is no clear evidence for this. Intravenous steroid is used to help faster recovery, but the extent of recovery and the effect on relapse rate are unchanged.

questions.question_text: Among the following options, which is not a key diagnostic feature of delirium?
questions.explanation: According to Criterion B of Delirium, the disturbance develops over a short period of time, usually hours to a few days. It also tends to fluctuate through the day, often worsening in the evening and at night. Mild and major neurocognitive disorders that increase the risk of delirium usually have a chronic course.

questions.question_text: A 72-year-old man with no prior diagnosis of alcohol or other substance use disorders and no psychiatric history is brought to the emergency department (ED) because of transient episodes of unexplained loss of consciousness. His wife reports that he has experienced repeated falls and syncope over the past year, as well as auditory and visual hallucinations. A thorough workup for cardiac disease has found no evidence of structural heart disease or arrhythmias. In the ED, he is found to have severe autonomic dysfunction, encompassing orthostatic hypotension and urinary incontinence. What is the best provisional diagnosis for this patient?

options.text: A diagnosis of new-onset Parkinson disease.
A diagnosis of new-onset essential tremor.
Possible major or mild neurocognitive disorder with Lewy bodies.
Possible major or mild neurocognitive disorder due to Alzheimer’s disease.

correct_answer.text: Possible major or mild neurocognitive disorder with Lewy bodies.

questions.explanation: Further information on cognition, time frame, and other etiologies must be ascertained, but the best working diagnosis with the limited information available is neurocognitive disorder with Lewy bodies (NCDLB). Individuals with NCDLB frequently experience repeated falls and syncope and transient episodes of unexplained loss of consciousness. Severe autonomic dysfunction, such as orthostatic hypotension and urinary incontinence, may also be observed. Auditory and other nonvisual hallucinations are common, as are systematized delusions, delusional misidentification, and depression. The patient has auditory and visual hallucinations but no other feature of schizophrenia or schizoaffective disorder, and the age at onset, along with the associated neurological symptoms, suggest a neurodegenerative disorder rather than schizophrenia or schizoaffective illness. Among neurocognitive disorders, the prominence of hallucinations, episodic loss of consciousness, and autonomic symptoms in the early course—rather than marked memory impairment—argue against a neurocognitive disorder due to Alzheimer’s disease and in favor of NCDLB. The patient has one of the “core diagnostic features” of NCDLB, visual hallucinations, justifying a “possible” level of certainty for the diagnosis. A seizure disorder might cause episodic loss of consciousness but would not parsimoniously account for hallucinations and autonomic symptoms.

questions.question_text: What would be Accurate regarding psychosis in major neurocognitive disorder due to Alzheimer’s disease?

options.text: individuals with psychotic symptoms have a faster cognitive decline.
Psychotic symptoms are observed in roughly 10% of individuals.
occurrence rate of psychotic symptoms is consistent through the course of the disease.
Visual hallucinations are the most common psychotic symptom.
Psychotic symptoms are more prevalent than agitation.

correct_answer.text: individuals with psychotic symptoms have a faster cognitive decline.

questions.explanation: Patients with major neurocognitive disorder due to Alzheimer’s disease with associated psychosis have a faster rate of decline than patients without psychotic symptoms. Median prevalence of psychosis in major neurocognitive disorder due to Alzheimer’s disease is approximately 41%, although estimates range from 12.2% to 74.1%. Prevalence of psychotic symptoms increases with duration of illness. Delusions (often persecutory) are more common than hallucinations. Agitation is more prevalent than psychosis. questions.question_text: Which gait pattern is wide-based with truncal instability and irregular lurching steps?
questions.explanation: Ataxic gait is wide-based with truncal instability and irregular lurching steps resulting in lateral veering and, if severe, falling. This is classically seen in cerebellar disease, such as Wernicke's encephalopathy.

questions.question_text: What test is most appropriate to detect amyloid-beta and tau pathology in Alzheimer's disease?
questions.explanation: Immunochemical stain detects amyloid-beta and tau pathology in Alzheimer's disease tissue samples.

questions.question_text: A 25-year-old male presents with mild cognitive deficits and movement abnormality. Antibodies against which protein are most likely responsible?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of mild cognitive deficits with movement abnormality in a young adult is consistent with LGI1 (Leucine-rich glioma-inactivated protein 1) antibody encephalitis. Antibodies against neuronal cell surface or synaptic receptors like LGI1, NMDAR, AMPAR, and GABAR are typically treatable forms of autoimmune encephalitis.

questions.question_text: Which gait pattern is characterized by small, shuffling steps with a stooped forward posture?
questions.explanation: Festinating gait (also called shuffling gait) presents with a stooped posture, slow gait initiation, and small shuffling steps. This is classically associated with Parkinson's disease.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is NOT a type of fronto-temporal degeneration (FTD)?
questions.explanation: Huntington's disease is not a type of fronto-temporal degeneration. FTD includes behavioural variant FTD, primary progressive aphasia (Pick's disease), progressive non-fluent aphasia, semantic dementia, and logopenic progressive aphasia. PSP is no longer classified under FTD in ICD-11, being reclassified under atypical Parkinson's, though it overlaps with FTDs.

questions.question_text: Coiled bodies are seen in which condition:
questions.explanation: Coiled bodies are tau-positive inclusions found in astrocytes and oligodendrocytes, particularly in the substantia nigra, subthalamic nucleus, and globus pallidus. They are a characteristic microscopic feature of progressive supranuclear palsy.

questions.question_text: In which of the following types of aphasia is speech fluent, incomprehensible, with preserved repetition?
questions.explanation: Transcortical sensory aphasia involves damage to specific areas of the temporal lobe of the brain, resulting in symptoms such as poor auditory comprehension, relatively intact repetition, and fluent speech with semantic paraphasias present. It is a fluent aphasia similar to Wernicke's, with the exception of a strong ability to repeat words and phrases. In Broca's aphasia individuals have great difficulty forming complete sentences with generally only basic content words (leaving out words like is and the). In conduction aphasia individual can comprehend what is being said and is fluent in spontaneous speech, but they cannot repeat what is being said to them. Transcortical motor aphasia is characterized by non-fluent speech output, with good comprehension and repetition.

questions.question_text: An autopsy is performed on a 74yearold individual who had a 3year history of progressive cognitive decline. Based on the neuropathological findings, the pathologist concludes the individual likely suffered from major neurocognitive disorder with Lewy bodies. What is the neuropathological finding? Y BOARD REvIEw
questions.explanation: Lewy bodies are composed of alphasynuclein intracytoplasmic inclusions. These also may be observed in major neurocognitive disorder due to Parkinson disease. Amyloid plaques and neurofibrillary tangles are characteristic neuropathology in Alzheimer disease. Intranuclear eosinophilic inclusions, or Cowdry bodies, are seen in subacute sclerosing panencephalitis. Spongiform encephalopathy is seen in major neurocognitive disorder due to prion disease, such as Creutzfeldt– Jakob disease.

questions.question_text: Miriam Lossef was involved in a sporting accident resulting in damage to her frontal lobe. It seems as though the other areas of the brain remained intact. You conduct a number of tests to determine the extent of the damage. Which of the following is a localising sign for frontal lobe damage?
questions.explanation: A and D are parietal lobe signs, B and D are temporal lobe signs

questions.question_text: Which enzyme deficiency causes acute intermittent porphyria?
questions.explanation: Hydroxymethylbilane synthase (HMBS) deficiency causes acute intermittent porphyria.

questions.question_text: DIAGNOStIC AND C LINICAL EvALUAt similar attacks of double vision twice in the past year and carries a diagnosis of relapsing– remitting multiple sclerosis. She also has major depressive disorder and nonadherence with antidepressant medication. Which of the following is the most suitable treatment to delay disability for this individual?
questions.explanation: Sydenham chorea is seen most frequently in girls who have a history of Group A betahemolytic streptococcal infection/ rheumatic fever and is characterized by irregular movements of the limbs, trunk, and face. Movements occur as a result of autoantibodies attacking the basal ganglia. Most children recover. Pediatric acuteonset neuropsychiatric syndrome (PANS; until recently known as pediatric autoimmune neuropsychiatric disorder associated with streptococcal infection, or PANDAS) is also a disorder associated with Group A betahemolytic streptococcal infection; however, PANS is associated with onset of vocal and/ or motor tics. Tics in Tourette syndrome can usually be suppressed with effort and are stereotyped rather than irregular.

questions.question_text: A patient cannot perform a complex task like using a hammer but can perform each individual step. What is this called?
questions.explanation: Ideational apraxia is the inability to follow a sequence of actions in correct order, such as taking a match from a box and striking it properly.

questions.question_text: Among the following, which is not a feature of Binswanger’s disease?

options.text: A diagnosis of rapidly progressive dementia
Clinical signs may include parkinsonian syndrome
Subcortical white matter changes in periventricular and subcortical regions
characteristically seen in chronic hypertensive individuals

correct_answer.text: A diagnosis of rapidly progressive dementia

questions.explanation: Binswanger’s disease is a slowly progressive dementia associated with subacute progression of focal neurological defi cits in chronically hypertensive patients. These defi cits could involve pseudobulbar, pyramidal, and parkinsonian features. Incontinence and fl uctuating cognition may be seen. The periventricular area shows white matter demyelination, especially resulting from diffuse ischaemic damage. Lacunar infarcts are frequently absent. In patients thought to have multi-infarct dementia, leucoaraiosis is found in at least three quarters. Stein G and Wilkinson G. Seminars in General Adult Psychiatry, 2nd edn. RCPsych Publications, 2007, p. 516.

questions.question_text: A patient presents with memory issues for 8 months with suspected Alzheimer's disease. Which finding would suggest an alternative diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Preserved long-term memory would be atypical for Alzheimer's disease, where long-term memory is typically affected; this finding suggests an alternative diagnosis.

questions.question_text: A man who survived a severe road traffic accident 5 years ago presents to the clinic with ongoing, debilitating distress. He reports experiencing recurrent, vivid nightmares about the collision and suffers from intense physiological reactivity whenever he hears screeching tires. He actively avoids driving or riding in vehicles, states he feels constantly hypervigilant, and struggles with a heightened startle response and severe insomnia. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
According to the DSM-5-TR (Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition, Text Revision), a diagnosis of PTSD requires exposure to a traumatic event followed by specific symptom clusters that persist for more than one month and cause significant functional impairment.

This vignette maps directly to the established, evidence-based diagnostic criteria for PTSD:

Exposure to Trauma (Criterion A): The patient was involved in a severe road traffic accident, which constitutes a qualifying traumatic event involving actual or threatened death/serious injury.

Intrusion Symptoms (Criterion B): The patient experiences intrusive, involuntary memories of the event, demonstrated by the recurrent nightmares and the intense physical reactivity to trauma-related cues (screeching tires).

Avoidance (Criterion C): The patient actively alters his behavior to avoid stimuli associated with the trauma, shown by his refusal to drive or ride in vehicles.

Arousal and Reactivity (Criterion E): The trauma has led to marked alterations in arousal, evidenced by hypervigilance (feeling constantly \"on edge\"), an exaggerated startle response, and severe insomnia.
Duration (Criterion F): The event occurred 5 years ago, and the ongoing nature of these symptoms satisfies the requirement that the disturbance lasts for more than one month.

questions.question_text: What is the most important pathophysiological hallmark of Alzheimer's disease?
questions.explanation: The two most important pathophysiological hallmarks of Alzheimer's disease are beta-amyloid plaques that accumulate extracellularly and tau tangles that accumulate intracellularly.

questions.question_text: Which neurodegenerative disorder is linked to schizophrenia-like psychosis?
questions.explanation: Both Huntington's disease and Friedreich's ataxia are associated with schizophrenia-like psychosis. Huntington's disease presents with schizophrenia-like psychosis in 6-25% of patients, with paranoid form being most common. Friedreich's ataxia, an autosomal recessive spinocerebellar ataxia, has documented psychiatric manifestations including schizophrenia-like psychosis. Muscular dystrophy is not typically associated with schizophrenia-like features.

questions.question_text: Which protein inclusion is most commonly seen in frontotemporal dementia?
questions.explanation: The classification of frontotemporal dementias is based on protein inclusions. The most common inclusions contain tau, TDP-43 (a DNA/RNA-binding protein), or FUS (fused in sarcoma). Tau-positive, amyloid-negative is the most frequent pattern in FTD.

questions.question_text: Among the following, which is a feature of cognitive impairment in Huntington’s disease?

options.text: Loss of procedural memory from onset
Late-onset verbal memory and visuospatial impairment
Speech production is affected before speech comprehension

questions.explanation: Verbal recognition is relatively spared compared with recall, which suggests a retrieval problem rather than an encoding problem. Problems with verbal memory and visuospatial function appear early in Huntington’s disease, but don’t progress as much as in patients with Alzheimer’s. The picture is typical of a subcortical dementia involving frontal subcortical circuits. Patients with Huntington’s disease show a typical loss of procedural memory. Executive function is lost early in the disease. They also show psychomotor slowing and attentional defi cits that correlate with activities of daily living (ADL). Unlike psychiatric symptoms, cognitive symptoms correlate with the number of trinucleotide repeats. Speech comprehension is maintained late into the disease well after intelligible speech production is lost. Cummings JL and Mega MS. Neuropsychiatry and Behavioural Neuroscience, 2nd edn. Oxford University Press 2003, p. 272.

questions.question_text: A man had a motor vehicle accident 5 years ago and now presents with bilateral coarse tremors and impaired eye focusing (reduced gaze). Sleeping tablets temporarily improve his tremors. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of post-traumatic symptoms with tremor and oculomotor issues following significant trauma 5 years prior is most consistent with PTSD.

questions.question_text: Mr Keith Williams is a 40-year-old man with a history of alcohol dependence who is brought to the hospital by his family. They are concerned as he has been having difficulty walking and cannot remember any events over the last several days. Which of the following could be true for Mr Williams?
questions.explanation: The diagnosis is Wenicke-Korsakoff syndrome, which is associated with reduced activity of transketolase in the mammillary bodies. Transketolase activity is decreased in deficiency of thiamine, such as in Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome. There is an indication that thiamine deficiency leads to Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome only in those whose transketolase has a reduced affinity for thiamine. In this way, the activity of transketolase is greatly hindered, and, as a consequence, the entire pentose phosphate pathway is inhibited.

questions.question_text: An otherwise healthy 60yearold female patient who has been irritable and paranoid over the past week was brought to the emergency room by family after she had a tION OF N EUROLOGICAL DISORDERS • 153 witnessed seizure. EEG reveals cortical excitability over bilateral temporal lobes. On evaluation, she is unable to remember words for more than 30 seconds. Lumbar puncture reveals very slight lymphocytosis but is negative for herpes simplex virus (HSV). Which of the following is the most likely cause of her presentation?
questions.explanation: Limbic encephalitis is a clinical term that describes encephalitis with temporal lobe predilection; its classic triad includes anterograde amnesia due to hippocampal dysfunction, temporal lobe seizures due to inflammation, and a host of potential psychiatric symptoms. HSV encephalitis causes a limbic encephalitis, but because this has been ruled out, the next likely etiology is autoimmunity. Several antibodies have been implicated, including antiHu, anti– NMDA receptor, antiLGI1, and so forth. Identifying the specific antibody will guide management. Autoimmune limbic encephalitis has paraneoplastic and nonparaneoplastic variants. Several antibodies (such as antiHu) imply an associated malignancy, whereas others have a fairly weak association with malignancy (such as anti– NMDA receptors in males).

questions.question_text: Which gait pattern is characteristic of Huntington's disease?

options.text: Chaotic upper motor and scissoring lower motor gait with foot drop

correct_answer.text: Chaotic upper motor and scissoring lower motor gait with foot drop

questions.explanation: Huntington's disease presents with a characteristic chaotic gait involving both upper motor neuron signs and scissoring of the lower extremities, along with foot drop and high-stepping gait.

questions.question_text: What is the typical age range for LGI1 autoimmune encephalitis?
questions.explanation: LGI1 autoimmune encephalitis typically affects older adults, with the peak incidence in the 55-64 year age range.

questions.question_text: A 38yearold male patient comes to a neurologist for evaluation of gait changes because he has had several months of worsening restlessness and incoordination. He is observed to have jerky, random movements of his limbs. His wife reports that he has been more forgetful recently and is having trouble managing his finances. The individual’s father developed similar symptoms in his early 40s. What would be expected on MRI?
questions.explanation: The patient likely has Huntington disease, which is characterized by chorea, cognitive decline (particularly with executive function), behavioral abnormalities, psychosis, and depression with high risk of suicide. It is caused by an

questions.question_text: Histopathologically, Lewy bodies are intracellular cytoplasmic inclusions primarily composed of:
questions.explanation: Lewy bodies are weakly eosinophilic, spherical, intracellular cytoplasmic inclusions composed of alpha-synuclein. Antibody to the protease ubiquitin can also be used to identify them.

questions.question_text: Which aura occurs in occipital seizures?
questions.explanation: Occipital lobe seizures typically produce visual auras such as visual illusions or hallucinations.

questions.question_text: Which proteins are characteristically accumulated in frontotemporal dementia?
questions.explanation: Frontotemporal dementia is characterized by accumulation of ubiquitinated proteins and tau tangles, particularly in frontotemporal regions.

questions.question_text: Which gait pattern is described as feet seeming magnetically attracted to the floor?
questions.explanation: Magnetic gait, where feet seem as if magnetically attracted to the floor, is characteristically associated with normal pressure hydrocephalus.

questions.question_text: What is the best CSF marker for anti-NMDAR encephalitis?
questions.explanation: Anti-NMDA receptor antibodies in the cerebrospinal fluid are the most specific and sensitive diagnostic marker for anti-NMDAR encephalitis.

questions.question_text: A man is unable to follow a sequence of actions in the correct order, such as taking a match from a box and striking it. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Ideational apraxia is characterized by inability to follow a sequence of actions in the correct order, representing a breakdown in the conceptual knowledge of action sequences.

questions.question_text: What is the pathological finding in Alzheimer's disease?
questions.explanation: Beta amyloid plaques and tau neurofibrillary tangles are the hallmark pathological findings in Alzheimer's disease.

questions.question_text: Among the options below, which one conditions has overlapping features with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis?

options.text: Neurocognitive disorder due to Alzheimer disease
A diagnosis of vascular neurocognitive disorder
A diagnosis of frontotemporal neurocognitive disorder
Neurocognitive disorder due to Parkinson disease

correct_answer.text: A diagnosis of frontotemporal neurocognitive disorder

questions.explanation: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) and frontotemporal neurocognitive disorder (FTD) have overlapping presentations. Both ALS and FTD patients suffer from executive dysfunction, which is thought due to TARDNAbinding protein 43 (TDP43) inclusions in the hippocampus, amygdala, and spinal cord. TDP43 burden reflects clinical manifestations. Both conditions may share mechanisms of protein misfolding.

questions.question_text: What would be the approximate rate of depression among individuals with Parkinson’s disease?
questions.explanation: Depression is seen in up to 40% of patients with Parkinson’s disease. Re FeRe NCe Kimchi, E. Z., & Lyketsos, C. G. Dementia and mild neurocognitive disorders. In D. C. questions.question_text: A 58yearold female patient comes to a neurologist with rapidly progressing dementia for 2 months and irregular, shocklike muscle contractions. The neurologist performs an electroencephalogram (EEG), which shows periodic sharpwave complexes. What marker would be expected in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF)?
questions.explanation: Dementia and myoclonus in a middleaged adult is characteristic of mild and major neurocognitive disorder due to prion disease, in this case Creutzfeldt– Jakob disease. Classically in this disorder, EEG demonstrates periodic sharpwave complexes, and CSF is positive for 143- 3 protein. CSF amyloid protein is decreased and tau protein increased in major neurocognitive disorder due to Alzheimer disease. Positive VDRL would be seen in neurosyphilis. Increased measles antibody titer would be seen in subacute sclerosing panencephalitis. NMDA receptor antibody encephalitis may show a range of EEG changes, including diffuse background slowing or generalized cortical excitability, but the most specific EEG signature is extreme delta brush (alpha waves superimposed on delta waves).

questions.question_text: Among the following, which is a feature of amnestic mild cognitive impairment (MCI)?

options.text: Absence of memory impairment relative to age-matched healthy control
Presence of evidence of clinical dementia
Amyloid deposits and tau-positive tangles are seen more often in the mesial temporal lobes than in normal controls

correct_answer.text: Amyloid deposits and tau-positive tangles are seen more often in the mesial temporal lobes than in normal controls

questions.explanation: MCI is a syndrome characterized by the presence of cognitive decline greater than that expected for age and education level along with normal ADL. It is, thus, distinct from dementia, in which cognitive defi cits are more severe and widespread and have a signifi cant effect on daily function. A further subtype of MCI, amnestic subtype, has a higher rate of conversion to Alzheimer’s disease. They characterized by memory complaints, corroborated by an informant: the presence of memory impairment relative to age- and education-matched healthy people; typical general cognitive function; largely intact ADL; and not clinically demented. Prevalence in population-based epidemiological studies ranges from 3% to 19% in adults older than 65 years. Compared with people with dementia and normal controls, individuals with MCI have intermediate amounts of Alzheimer’s disease pathology, including amyloid deposition and tau-positive tangles in the mesial temporal lobes. Gauthier S, Reisberg B, Zaudig M, et al. Mild cognitive impairment. Lancet 367: 1262–1270.

questions.question_text: Among the following options, which neurocognitive disorders (NCDs) is especially distinguished by impairment in domains such as speech production, word finding, object naming, or word comprehension, whereas episodic memory, perceptual-motor abilities, and executive function are relatively preserved?

options.text: Major or mild NCD due to Alzheimer’s disease.
Major or mild NCD with Lewy bodies. Neurocognitive Disorders—QUESTIONS | 125
Behavioral-variant major or mild frontotemporal NCD.
Language-variant major or mild frontotemporal NCD.

correct_answer.text: Language-variant major or mild frontotemporal NCD.

questions.explanation: Major or mild frontotemporal NCD comprises a number of syndromic variants characterized by the progressive development of behavioral and personality change and/or language impairment. The behavioral variant Neurocognitive Disorders—ANSWER GUIDE | 419 and three language variants (semantic, agrammatic/nonfluent, and logopenic) exhibit distinct patterns of brain atrophy and some distinctive neuropathology. The criteria must be met for either the behavioral or the language variant to make the diagnosis, but many individuals present with features of both. Individuals with language-variant major or mild frontotemporal NCD present with primary progressive aphasia with gradual onset, with three subtypes commonly described: semantic variant, agrammatic/nonfluent variant, and logopenic variant, and each variant has distinctive features and corresponding neuropathology. Individuals with behavioral-variant major or mild frontotemporal NCD present with varying degrees of apathy or disinhibition. They may lose interest in socialization, self-care, and personal responsibilities, or display socially inappropriate behaviors. Insight is usually impaired, and this often delays medical consultation. The first referral is often to a psychiatrist. Individuals may develop changes in social style, and in religious and political beliefs, with repetitive movements, hoarding, changes in eating behavior, and hyperorality. In later stages, loss of sphincter control may occur. Cognitive decline is less prominent, and formal testing may show relatively few deficits in the early stages. Common neurocognitive symptoms are lack of planning and organization, distractibility, and poor judgment. Deficits in executive function, such as poor performance on tests of mental flexibility, abstract reasoning, and response inhibition, are present, but learning and memory are relatively spared, and perceptual motor abilities are almost always preserved in the early stages.

questions.question_text: Which aura occurs in parietal lobe seizures?
questions.explanation: Parietal lobe seizures typically produce somatosensory auras, including numbness, tingling, or other somatic sensations.

questions.question_text: Lecanemab is indicated for Alzheimer's disease treatment only in patients with which finding?
questions.explanation: Lecanemab treatment was initiated in participants with mild cognitive impairment or mild dementia who had confirmed presence of amyloid-beta pathology.

questions.explanation: Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML) is a severe, fatal demyelinating brain disease caused by the polyoma JC virus.
