questions.question_text: Andrew is a 30-year-old man who presented with frontal headaches and a history of complex partial seizures. characteristically, his seizures begin with 20 seconds of orobuccal movements followed by 40 seconds of altered consciousness. At seizure onset, Andrew feels he must constantly think of the word ‘Supercalifragilisticexpialidocious’ and repeat this several times without him being able to control it. What is this phenomenon called?
questions.explanation: This type of psychic aura is called ‘forced thinking,’ characterized by recurrent intrusive thoughts, ideas, or crowding of thoughts. Forced thinking must be distinguished from obsessional thoughts and compulsive urges. Epileptic patients with forced thinking experience their thoughts as stereotypical, out-of-context, brief, and irrational, but not necessarily as ego dystonic. Periodic lateralizations are recurrent EEG complexes that may be associated with prolonged confusional behaviour and focal cognitive changes. Kaplan HI. Kaplan and Sadock’s Comprehensive Textbook of Psychiatry, 8th edn. Lippincott Williams and Wilkins, 2004; p. 381.

questions.question_text: Which treatment is most effective for HIV encephalitis?
questions.explanation: Prompt administration of antiretroviral therapy is the most effective treatment for HIV encephalitis and associated neurocognitive dysfunction.

questions.question_text: Which protein pathology is characteristic of tau-positive frontotemporal dementia?
questions.explanation: Tau-positive FTD (often Pick's disease) shows tau tangles and Pick bodies; this is associated with MAPT gene mutations.

questions.question_text: A 28yearold adopted male with major depression and history of two serious suicide attempts is ultimately presenting with a diagnosis of Huntington’s disease after he developed clumsiness, falls, and athetotic movements. He comes to the clinic for worsening choreiform movements. He is currently euthymic on fluoxetine. Which of the following is critical that the individual knows before starting tetrabenazine?

options.text: It is available under a humanitarian use exemption by the FDA.
Its use is offlabel for Huntington’s disease.
It may be more effective for athetosis than for choreiform movements.
It carries a black box warning for risk of depression and suicidality.

correct_answer.text: It carries a black box warning for risk of depression and suicidality.

questions.explanation: Tetrabenazine is the only FDAapproved medication for Huntington’s disease, specifically for chorea. It is recommended as firstline treatment for Huntington’s chorea. It does carry a black box warning for worsening depression and suicidality because it depletes monoamines. Other agents, including antipsychotics (some evidence for olanzapine, risperidone, and aripiprazole), amantadine, and riluzole, may be considered if tetrabenazine is ineffective or contraindicated. Tetrabenazine is metabolized via 2D6, and patients requiring doses more than 50 mg/ day should be genotyped for CYP2D6.

questions.question_text: What is the best management for HIV-related cognitive impairment?
questions.explanation: Antiretroviral therapy targeting viral replication is the best management for HIV-related cognitive impairment, as it reduces CNS viral load and improves cognitive function.

questions.question_text: Which statement is true about confabulation?

options.text: There is subjective awareness of memory loss
Can only occur in Korsakoff syndrome
There is deliberate falsification of facts

questions.explanation: In confabulation, autobiographical memory is affected, though not always uniformly. Confabulation is not exclusive to Korsakoff syndrome and can occur in various conditions including clouded consciousness. It is typically not deliberate falsification but rather unconscious filling in of memory gaps. While sometimes there may be subjective awareness, this is not always present.

questions.question_text: A 20yearold obese female patient comes to the emergency room for headache. On exam, she demonstrates papilledema. A neurologist performs a lumbar puncture and finds the opening pressure to be 285 mm cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) The individual’s headache improves after repeated lumbar puncture. Her presentation is most consistent with:

options.text: Spinal cord tumor with mass effect

questions.explanation: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension (previously known as pseudotumor cerebri) characteristically affects young obese women. Lumbar puncture reveals elevated CSF pressure greater than 250 mm CSF. Headache is associated with increased intracranial pressure in that it develops concurrently with and/ or is aggravated by the increased intracranial pressure or is relieved by reducing intracranial pressure.

questions.question_text: Which autoimmune encephalitis is characterized by faciobrachial dystonic seizures and hyponatremia in elderly males?
questions.explanation: Anti-LGI1 encephalitis typically presents in elderly males with faciobrachial dystonic seizures and hyponatremia as characteristic features.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is NOT a type of familial frontotemporal dementia?
questions.explanation: Huntington's disease is not a variant of familial frontotemporal dementia; it is a separate neurodegenerative disorder caused by mutations in the HTT gene on chromosome 4, while FTD variants are caused by mutations in GRN, MAPT, or C9orf72.

questions.question_text: Which gait pattern is most characteristic of normal pressure hydrocephalus?
questions.explanation: Normal pressure hydrocephalus is characterized by a magnetic gait, where patients appear to shuffle with their feet as if glued to the ground.

questions.question_text: An HIV patient with cognitive disorder on long-term antiretroviral therapy (ART) is found to have neuronal loss on neuropathological examination. Which neuropathological change is most consistent with this finding?
questions.explanation: Despite suppression of viral replication with long-term ART, HIV-associated cognitive impairment can still occur due to neuronal loss and damage. Neuropathological examination reveals evidence of neuronal loss, which correlates with cognitive dysfunction.

questions.question_text: Which condition is characterized by inherited prion disease in humans?
questions.explanation: Familial fatal insomnia is an inherited human prion disease caused by a point mutation in the prion protein gene, characterized by progressive insomnia and autonomic dysfunction.

questions.question_text: Among the following options, which remain(s) intact in persistent vegetative states?

options.text: Wakefulness with ability to follow commands
Ability to respond to painful stimuli

questions.explanation: Individuals with persistent vegetative state do open their eyes but are not able to track or interact meaningfully with the people around them. Vital functions such s digestion, breathing, sleeping, and maintaining temperature remain in persistent vegetative state.

questions.question_text: A 10-year-old boy with a prior diagnosis of dyslexia, who is otherwise developmentally normal, is in a skateboarding accident in which he experiences severe traumatic brain injury. This results in significant global intellectual impairment (with a persistent reading deficit that is more pronounced than his other newly acquired but stable deficits, along with a full-scale IQ of 75). There is mild impairment in his adaptive behavior such that he requires support in some areas of functioning. He is also displaying anxious and depressive symptoms in response to his accident and hospitalization. What is the least likely diagnosis?

options.text: Specific learning disorder is the appropriate diagnosis given the pronounced reading deficit.
A diagnosis of traumatic brain injury.
A diagnosis of specific learning disorder.
Major neurocognitive disorder due to traumatic brain injury.

correct_answer.text: Major neurocognitive disorder due to traumatic brain injury.

questions.explanation: There are no exclusion criteria for a diagnosis of intellectual developmental disorder in DSM-5, which notes that both specific learning disorder and communication disorders can co-occur if the criteria are met. Although his full-scale IQ is 75, the statistical model associated with his intellect would allow for his actual IQ to be (cid:114)5 points. His adaptive functioning would be the key factor in his receiving the diagnosis of intellectual developmental disorder, with a mild level of severity due to needing to receive only some support in most of his areas of functioning. With his reading skills remaining disproportionately impaired in comparison with the rest of his cognitive profile, and because onset of these impairments was during the developmental period, he would continue to receive a diagnosis of specific learning disorder (dyslexia). His emotional symptoms in response to the accident would yield a potential diagnosis of an adjustment disorder. The boy’s deficits are not severe enough to qualify for a diagnosis of major neurocognitive disorder.

questions.question_text: Which dementia is typically tau-positive and amyloid-negative?
questions.explanation: Frontotemporal dementia, including Pick's disease, is characteristically tau-positive and amyloid-negative.

questions.question_text: A HIV carrier with ring like lesions on MRI scan is most likely to have a diagnosis of
questions.explanation: Cerebral toxoplasmosis commonly affects patients with advanced HIV immunodeficiency. Toxoplasmosis in patients who are immunocompromised can be severe and debilitating in patients with Central Nervous System (CNS) involvement, and the condition may be fatal. Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) scan shows multiple ring enhancing lesions with extensive surrounding oedema in supratentorial as well as the infratentorial region.

questions.question_text: Charles Bonnet syndrome is associated with
questions.explanation: Charles Bonnet syndrome: Elderly patients, with normal consciousness and no brain pathology, with reduced visual acuity due to ocular problems, experience vivid, distinct, usually well-coloured (in contrast to real sensation that is blurred due to eye disease) formed hallucinations – mostly humans, at times animals and cartoons. These objects usually show movement, and can be voluntarily controlled – disappear on closing the eyes; insight about unreality is usually preserved – though they may evoke emotions including fear and joy. About 1/3rd are elementary; usually the hallucinations are located in external space.

questions.question_text: Which feature is not associated with supranuclear palsy?
questions.explanation: The most common early complaint in progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP) is unsteadiness of gait and unexplained falling (retropulsion). It may take a year or longer for the characteristic syndrome-comprising supranuclear ophthalmoplegia, pseudobulbar palsy, and axial dystonia to develop fully. They may have difficulty in voluntary vertical movement of the eyes (vertical gaze palsy). The principal areas of the brain affected are: the basal ganglia, the brainstem, particularly the portion of the midbrain where supranuclear eye movement resides, the cerebral cortex and the dentate nucleus of the cerebellum. The neurons display neurofibrillary tangles, which are clumps of tau protein.

questions.question_text: A 59-year-old gentleman is being assessed in the memory clinic. He presents with progressive loss of memory for 'words' but has good day-to-day memory for events. What is his most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: In patients with frontotemporal dementia, there is a relative preservation of day-to-day memory (episodic). The temporal lobe variant presents more commonly with semantic dementia, a syndrome of progressive word finding difficulty, loss of language comprehension, depletion of conceptual knowledge and impairment of object recognition.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is INCORRECT with regard to vegetative states?

options.text: Cycles of eye closure and opening are absent
Complete absence of awareness of environment

correct_answer.text: Cycles of eye closure and opening are absent

questions.explanation: Monti et al. provided a set of criteria for diagnosing vegetative states: Three main clinical features define the vegetative state: (a) cycles of eye opening and closing

questions.question_text: In delirium, which of the following domains of orientation is the first to be affected?
questions.explanation: Orientation is usually assessed for time, place and person; it is not a particularly sensitive cognitive test. Intact orientation does not exclude a significant memory disorder, particularly if there is concern about memory in the history from an informant. Time orientation is the most helpful, affected early in delirium and the test should include a question on the time of the day (Kipps and Hodges (2006). questions.question_text: A 66-year-old patient is incidentally diagnosed to have a carotid bruit. Which of the following can be expected if he develops a thromboembolism?
questions.explanation: Amaurosis fugax is loss of vision in one eye due to a temporary lack of blood flow to the retina. It may be a sign of an impending stroke.

questions.question_text: The type of amnesia seen in Korsakoff's syndrome is
questions.explanation: Korsakoff's syndrome is characterized by anterograde amnesia, retrograde amnesia with episodic memory impairment, confabulation, lack of insight and apathy. The retrograde amnesia extends back at least 25 to 30 years and includes loss of memory for remote information and autobiographical memory for incidents or events from the patient's past.

questions.question_text: Which of the following tests can differentiate organic from psychiatric stuporous states?
questions.explanation: Caloric testing in organic stupor will usually reveal tonic deviation whereas in a psychiatric stupor (catatonia/depression) ocular nystagmus will be present. This is because the fast phase reflects the ion following tonic deviation, and this requires the patient to be conscious (Retrieved from http://jnnp.bmj.com/content/71/suppl_1/i18.full).

questions.question_text: A construction worker sustains a head injury after a sudden fall. Following this he presents with a change in behaviour, violent outbursts, impulsivity and reduced speech fluency. Which of the following could be the most likely MRI finding in this patient?
questions.explanation: There are four regions of the prefrontal corex that are frequently mentioned in the scientific literature. These are orbitofrontal, dorsolateral prefrontal, anterior cingulate cortex and ventromedial cortex (the latter two together form the medial frontal surface). Pseudopsychopathy is a result of orbitofrontal damage.

questions.question_text: Mr. Phipps is 69 years old, with a history of depression, hypertension and hypercholesterolaemia. Last week he suffered a stroke affecting his nondominant occipitoparietal lobe. You draw Mr. Phipps' attention to objects on a table (a watch, a spoon, and a plant) and ask him to name them. He tells you he can see a spoon, but nothing else. When you redirect his attention to the plant, he says that now he does see the plant, but that he no longer sees the spoon. What term best describes this presentation?
questions.explanation: Simultanagnosia (also called simultagnosia) is a rare neurological disorder characterized by the inability of an individual to perceive more than one single object at a time, and is associated with occipito-parietal lesions.

questions.question_text: A 55-year-old heavy alcoholic was admitted to the medical ward after sustaining a major fall. He has severe Anterograde amnesia and extensive retrograde memory loss. However his working memory and procedural memory are unimpaired. What is his most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Korsakoff's syndrome: It is a form of an amnesic syndrome often occurring in patients with a history of severe alcohol abuse leading to thiamine deficiency. The patient may have severe Anterograde amnesia and extensive retrograde memory loss. This retrograde memory loss includes autobiographical memory loss with relative sparing of the most distant memories. Working memory and procedural memory are unimpaired. The pathological features are mostly found in paraventricular and periaqueductal grey matter, thalamus and mamillary bodies.

questions.question_text: The male: female ratio of pure frontal lobe degeneration is
questions.explanation: Frontotemporal lobe degeneration is characterized by progressive neuronal loss involving the frontal and or temporal lobes. The signs and symptoms often manifest between the ages of 55 and 65. 15% of those with FTD also have MND i.e. Motor Neuron Disease (also called Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis, ALS). MND with or without FTD is slightly more likely to be seen in men than women, but the difference is small. Population studies show nearly equal distribution by gender for pure frontal lobe degeneration and FTD without MND.

questions.question_text: You are seeing an elderly man with a history of low mood. He says he was feeling well until 18 months ago but progressively became low in his mood since then. He also complains of becoming more forgetful over the last year. However, he has no problem sleeping and appetite remains reasonably stable. Few months ago, he woke up suddenly with a limp and has been suffering from it since then. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Vascular insufficiency in the elderly is often associated with both cognitive impairment and depression that can be difficult to treat.

questions.question_text: Detection of 14-3-3 proteins in the CSF supports the diagnosis of
questions.explanation: The analysis of 14-3-3 proteins in the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) was shown to be highly sensitive and specific for the diagnosis of Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (CJD). In sporadic CJD, this test is helpful to support the diagnosis.

questions.question_text: What is the time duration before which most cases with acute uncomplicated delirium recover?
questions.explanation: Most cases of delirium recover in 4 weeks; in chronic lung disease, SABE (subacute bacterial endocarditis) and carcinoma up to 6 months long delirium may be seen

questions.question_text: A 23-year-old man is hospitalized for a fever of unknown origin and persistent cough. He also complains of being increasingly forgetful and having difficulties driving through familiar routes. Physical examination reveals several needle marks in his forearms. The most likely diagnosis is
questions.explanation: Needle marks, persistent cough and fever of unknown origin are suggestive of a HIV infection. Cognitive symptoms suggest HIV dementia.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is the best test to differentiate delirium from dementia?
questions.explanation: Dementia is not usually associated with altered consciousness unless there is a superimposed delirium, or if the patient is in an advanced state of profound dementia.

questions.question_text: Teichopsic hallucinations are typical of
questions.explanation: Teichopsia is also known as scintillating scotoma; it is the sensation of a luminous appearance before the eyes, with a zigzag, wall-like outline seen in migraine.

questions.question_text: The most common type of seizure with an aura is
questions.explanation: Episodes of temporal lobe disturbance (complex partial seizures) are often heralded by an aura involving an unpleasant odour such as burning paint or rubber.

questions.question_text: Epileptic automatism is associated with

options.text: Duration lasting few seconds to few minutes

correct_answer.text: Duration lasting few seconds to few minutes

questions.explanation: In the presence of disturbed consciousness, but preserved muscle tone and postural ability, patients with temporal lobe epilepsy may sometimes carry out complex motor acts termed as epileptic automatisms. These are usually shortlived.

questions.question_text: A 78-year-old man hospitalized after a fall, repeatedly sees small angels flying around his head. Which of the following is least likely to be true in this case?

options.text: This phenomenon can occur due to anticholinergic toxicity
This phenomenon is reported in delirium tremens
The perception has occurred without appropriate stimulus
This phenomenon is associated with organic disorders of the brain
Presence of intact consciousness suggests a functional disorder than an organic mental

correct_answer.text: Presence of intact consciousness suggests a functional disorder than an organic mental

questions.explanation: Auditory hallucinations are more characteristic of schizophrenic illnesses while visual hallucinations are characteristic of organic illnesses. Visual hallucinations are rarely seen as an isolated feature in psychotic illness. They are associated with organic disorders of the brain, cortical tumours, dementias, drug and alcohol intoxication and withdrawal, stimulant and hallucinogen ingestion and most commonly in delirium tremens.

questions.question_text: Regarding pure word deafness, which one of the following statements is false?

options.text: Here a patient can speak fluently.
The patient cannot understand speech, even though hearing is unimpaired for other
It is also called as sub cortical auditory dysphasia.
The patient can recognize the meaning of words.

correct_answer.text: The patient can recognize the meaning of words.

questions.explanation: Also called as subcortical auditory dysphasia, pure word deafness is characterized by the patient being able to speak, read and write fluently. But he cannot understand speech, even though hearing is unimpaired for other sounds; he hears words as sounds, but cannot recognize the meaning even though he knows that they are words.

questions.question_text: A 32-year-old shift worker presents with a history of headaches occurring in the mornings for a few months. His GP has been treating him for a diagnosis of tension headache. Which of the following features suggest a different pathology?

options.text: The localisation of pain is vague.
Associated with low mood and anxiety

questions.explanation: Postural change may indicate intracranial pathology.

questions.question_text: Neurofibrillary tangles are most commonly present in which of the following locations in Alzheimer's?
questions.explanation: Neurofibrillary tangles occur with ageing and in all the other conditions listed above. NFTs are found in the hippocampus (Ammons horn) and are also found in the Amygdala, parahippocampal gyrus, neocortex, locus coereleus, and nucleus of meynert and Raphe nuclei. Senile Plaques are found in the same sites as those of NFTs. Plaques include extra cellular Amyloid as a component, and beta A-4 protein is a major biochemical component of plaque Amyloid.

questions.question_text: Neurofibrillary tangles seen in Alzheimer's disease are made up of
questions.explanation: Neurofibrillary tangles are composed of cytoskeletal elements, primarily abnormally hyperphosphorylated tau protein. Tau is a peptide required for microtubule assembly. Microtubules are essential to transport of materials down axons. Hyperphosphorylation of Tau proteins can result in the self-assembly of tangles of paired helical filaments and straight filaments, which are involved in the pathogenesis of Alzheimer's disease.

questions.question_text: In pure word blindness which of the following is true?
questions.explanation: Also called subcortical visual aphasia, pure word blindness is associated with reduced reading comprehension but the patient can normally speak and understand the spoken word; he/she can write spontaneously and to dictation.

questions.question_text: Which of the following antidementia drugs acts directly on nicotine receptors?
questions.explanation: Galantamine, unlike the other anticholinesterases in clinical use, is derived from the alkaloids from the daffodil and snowdrop family. It is a reversible, competitive inhibitor of acetylcholinesterase with some inhibitory action on butyrylcholinesterase. It is also an agonist at nicotinic receptor sites. Although a clinically effective drug, galantamine frequently causes gastrointestinal side effects.

questions.question_text: Mr. Ellison is a 70-year-old man who was taken to his GP with increasing symptoms of cognitive impairment, resting tremor, limb stiffness and episodes when he appears to be seeing distressing things. Which of the following is the gene product most likely to be associated with his diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The diagnosis is Lewy body dementia (LBD) and the pathological finding in this condition is the presence of Lewy bodies. A Lewy body is an eosinophilic cytoplasmic inclusion consisting of a dense core surrounded by a halo of radiating fibrils. They are primarily composed of alpha-synuclein.

questions.question_text: There are various histological findings that are associated with organic brain disorders. Which of the following histological features are described as being carrot-shaped eosinophilic intracellular inclusions?
questions.explanation: Rosenthal fibres are thick, elongated (resemble a sausage, or carrot or corkscrew) eosinophilic bundle that can be found in the context of long-standing gliosis, low-grade gliomas, and some metabolic disorders. Lewy bodies are eosinophilic cytoplasmic inclusions consisting of a dense core surrounded by a halo of 10nm wide radiating fibrils. Hirano bodies are often described as rod-shaped, crystal-like, and eosinophilic and can be present in Alzheimer's disease and CJD.

questions.question_text: Which of the following gene products is associated with Frontotemporal dementia?
questions.explanation: Familial fronto-temporal dementia is associated with mutations in three genes: C9ORF72, tau protein (MAPT) and progranulin (PRG). Amyloid beta protein is associated with Alzhiemer's disease. Alpha and Beta-synuclein are found in Parkinson's disease. Alpha-synuclein is associated with Lewy body dementia. Gamma-synculein is found primarily in the paeripheral nervous system and is associated with breast tumour development.
